sources: Bord, Janet, and Colin Bord. The Secret Country: An interpretation of the folklore of ancient sites in the British Isles. New York: Walker and Co., 1976.
Straffon, Cheryl. The Earth Goddess: Celtic and Pagan Legacy of the Landscape. London: Blandford, 1997.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Fogous are underground stone chambers dug in Cornwall. Writers date their construction from about 500 years before the common era to about 500 years after it. They appear to be places used for ritual. Celts occupied the region in the later part of that span, so they may have built or used the chambers. Evidence also points to an older, pre-Celtic spiritual outlook. Many fogous align with the sunrise of the summer solstice. That line of stone suggests a calendar different from the one the Celts kept. Some writers see the chambers as a later echo of the megalithic culture that shaped Stonehenge. Legends tie the fogous to unearthly women, some read as goddesses. These beehive-shaped sites often hide secret inner chambers. Speculative reconstructions set initiation or other ceremonies in the small chambers.
